Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

can you turn these notes into clear step by step instructions for running the coat swap, not just a short event blurb. it’s a fictional neighborhood event and these are the details we have. please make it useful to the volunteers who will be there and to someone writing the information for visitors. keep the things we haven’t decided open rather than deciding for us.

1. when and where. the swap is on Saturday, November 14, at the Cedar Room in Westbank Community Centre. the room is available to our group starting at 8:30 a.m. volunteers should arrive at 8:45. the public event is 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. people bringing coats can drop them off from 9:30 to 10, but doors for the swap itself open at 10. at 1 we stop admitting people, then volunteers pack up until 2. don’t add a year, we have not given one.

2. what the swap is for. it is free and open to anyone in the neighborhood, and no one has to prove income or explain why they need a coat. somebody may bring a coat and leave without choosing one, or come without a coat and take one. please don’t describe it as an exchange where a coat has to be brought to get one. we are collecting winter coats only, adult and youth sizes, in any style. not hats, gloves, boots, scarves or other clothing. all genders and sizes are welcome. there is no cash table or charge. the short line we want to use on a sign is “Please take a coat that will keep you warm.”

3. what can be brought. coats should be clean and dry and wearable. we don’t want coats that are wet, smell of mildew, have heavy stains, or are torn or badly damaged. a small missing button is okay, but volunteers are not meant to repair anything. there may be coats without a size label; we can put those in an approximate-size area if the size seems clear, but don’t guess when it doesn’t. someone asked whether we should accept rain jackets, and we haven’t decided, so leave that as an open question rather than saying yes or no. we do not have bags to give out, so remind visitors they may want to bring their own bag, without making it a condition.

4. room and equipment. use four rolling racks for coats and eight tables for intake, folding, and smaller groupings by size. there are two mirrors and one folding screen for trying coats on. the centre has an accessible restroom nearby; we don’t have a separate private changing room. keep a clear route from the entrance to the racks and the restroom, and don’t put boxes in the doorway. masking tape and markers are available for temporary size signs. don’t make up a floor plan or claim we have more equipment.

5. people and sorting. there are six volunteers: two at intake, two to hang and sort coats, one near the mirrors, and one floater who can help where a line forms. when a coat arrives, intake checks the basic condition and sets aside coats that don’t meet the rules; the sorting volunteers group wearable coats by adult or youth and then by labeled size when possible. put unlabeled coats in the approximate-size area only if it’s clear. we have not decided what to do with rejected coats, so the instructions should say to set them aside and ask the coordinator, not throw them away or promise they’ll be returned. the coordinator’s note to volunteers says, “If you are unsure, pause and ask me rather than making up a rule.”

6. choosing coats. visitors may look through the racks and try coats on at the screen and mirrors. the current limit is one coat per person during the first hour, from 10 to 11. after noon, a person may take up to two if plenty remain. we haven’t decided what the limit is from 11 a.m. to noon, and “if plenty remain” has no numeric definition. flag both points for the coordinator; don’t fill in a rule. children may choose a coat with an adult present. no one should be required to explain their choice or take only a particular size.

7. information and end of event. please include what volunteers should do at setup, during arrival and intake, while visitors choose coats, at the 1 p.m. closing, and during packing through 2 p.m. we haven’t made a decision about leftover coats, and there is no named donation partner, so don’t say where they will go. there is no bad-weather cancellation plan in these notes. make the visitor information welcoming and straightforward, and identify those unresolved questions separately so we can answer them later. don’t add a phone number, registration, childcare, translation service, or emergency contact that hasn’t been provided.", "output": "Write clear, practical step-by-step instructions for running the fictional neighborhood winter coat swap described below. Make the instructions useful to the six volunteers on site, and include a separate section of visitor-facing information. Keep undecided details open: flag them as questions for the coordinator rather than supplying an answer. Do not add a year, equipment, services, rules, or other information not provided here.

1. Event time and location
- The swap takes place on Saturday, November 14, in the Cedar Room at Westbank Community Centre. No year has been provided.
- The room is available from 8:30 a.m.; volunteers should arrive at 8:45 a.m.
- Coat drop-off is from 9:30 to 10 a.m. The public swap runs from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Stop admitting people at 1 p.m.; volunteers pack up until 2 p.m.

2. Purpose and participation
- The event is free and open to anyone in the neighborhood. Visitors do not have to prove income or explain why they need a coat.
- People may bring a coat without taking one, or take a coat without bringing one. Do not describe the event as requiring an item in exchange.
- The swap is for winter coats only, in adult and youth sizes and any style, for all genders and sizes. Hats, gloves, boots, scarves, and other clothing are not included. There is no cash table or charge.
- Use this sign text exactly: “Please take a coat that will keep you warm.”

3. Coat condition and intake
- Accept coats that are clean, dry, and wearable. Do not accept coats that are wet, smell of mildew, have heavy stains, or are torn or badly damaged. A small missing button is acceptable; volunteers are not expected to repair coats.
- Group coats by adult or youth and by labeled size where possible. If a coat has no size label, place it in the approximate-size area only when its size is clear; do not guess otherwise.
- Rain jackets are an open question. Do not state whether they are accepted; flag this for the coordinator.
- Set aside coats that do not meet the condition rules and ask the coordinator what to do with them. Do not say they will be discarded or returned. The coordinator’s note is: “If you are unsure, pause and ask me rather than making up a rule.”
- Visitors may want to bring their own bags. There are no bags to give out, but bringing a bag is not a condition of participation.

4. Room and equipment
- Use four rolling racks for coats and eight tables for intake, folding, and smaller groupings by size. There are two mirrors and one folding screen for trying on coats.
- An accessible restroom is nearby. There is no separate private changing room.
- Keep the route from the entrance to the racks and restroom clear; do not leave boxes in the doorway. Masking tape and markers are available for temporary size signs. Do not invent a floor plan or additional equipment.

5. Volunteer roles
There are six volunteers: two at intake, two to hang and sort coats, one near the mirrors, and one floater to help where a line forms. Include these roles in the instructions without adding staff or assigning duties not supported by the notes.

6. Selecting coats and unresolved limits
Visitors may browse the racks and try on coats at the folding screen and mirrors. The current limit is one coat per person from 10 to 11 a.m. After noon, each person may take up to two coats if plenty remain. The limit from 11 a.m. to noon is undecided, and “if plenty remain” has no numeric definition. Flag both questions for the coordinator; do not supply a limit or define “plenty.” Children may choose a coat with an adult present. Visitors do not have to explain their choices or take only a particular size.

7. Requested coverage and open questions
Organize the instructions around setup, arrival and intake, visitors choosing coats, the 1 p.m. closing, and packing through 2 p.m. Include welcoming, straightforward visitor-facing information. Separately list the unresolved questions: whether rain jackets are accepted; what to do with rejected coats; the selection limit from 11 a.m. to noon; what counts as “plenty” after noon; what happens to leftover coats; and whether there is a bad-weather cancellation plan. No donation partner has been named.
